name: nest
desc: Neural Simulation Tool (NEST) with Python3 bindings (PyNEST)
why: NEST simulates spiking neural networks with PyNEST bindings, a real scientific tool you can run at home.

brief.what_it_is: NEST is an open-source simulator for spiking neural network models. It focuses on the dynamics, size and structure of neural systems rather than the detailed morphology of individual neurons. You describe a network in Python through PyNEST, or drive the stand-alone nest application, and the simulation runs in NEST's C++ kernel. It provides over 50 neuron models and over 10 synapse models, including Tsodyks-Markram short-term plasticity and several STDP variants.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames NEST as a way to follow the logic of an electrophysiological experiment inside a computer, where the experimenter defines the neural system being investigated. It is aimed at networks of spiking neurons of any size, such as cortical models, balanced random networks, and models of learning and plasticity.
brief.how_it_works: You define neurons and synapses, plus devices that stimulate or measure, much as a lab would set up instruments, then run the simulation. Connectivity is stored as an adjacency list rather than a weight matrix, so any two neurons can have several connections with different properties. You can inspect and modify the state of each neuron and connection during a run, and devices write their data to memory or to file.

commands_seen.context: Quick install of NEST from PyPI, per the README's Installation section.
macOS only: installs the OpenMP runtime, which the README says is needed for NEST's multithreading to work correctly. Run before the pip install.

brief.install_notes: README quick install is pip install nest-simulator; the README links a pip-install documentation page for more options. On macOS, install libomp with Homebrew first. The homepage says NEST needs only a C++ compiler and everything else is optional. Homebrew formula metadata (not the README) says PyNEST and its dependencies are installed with the python@3.15 formula, and that to use PyNEST you should use the Python interpreter at $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/python@3.15/bin, possibly adding that directory to your PATH. Installed executables are nest-config, nest-server and nest-server-mpi.
brief.standout: Connectivity is an adjacency list that allows multiple differently-parameterised connections between the same pair of neurons, rather than a single weight matrix. The project also says it has run since 1994 under the name SYNOD, and it is designed to scale from a laptop to supercomputers.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage lists the current release as NEST 3.10 (June 2026). The GitHub README carries CI, DOI and package badges for Ubuntu PPA, Fedora, conda-forge, Homebrew and Docker. I did not see a last-commit date or release history on the pages I read, so the exact date of the latest commit is unknown.
brief.caveats: Licensed under GPL v2 or later, which matters if you want to embed it in closed software. Runs on UNIX-like systems; the homepage says from MacBooks to BlueGene supercomputers. On macOS, multithreading needs libomp. Its focus is network-level dynamics, not detailed single-neuron morphology. The homepage's example list was truncated in my fetch, so I did not verify individual example contents.
quotes: NEST is a simulator for spiking neural network models that focuses on the dynamics, size and structure of neural systems rather than on the exact morphology of individual neurons.
NEST has minimal dependencies. All it really needs is a C++ compiler. Everything else is optional.

A NEST simulation tries to follow the logic of an electrophysiological experiment that takes place inside a computer with the difference that the neural system to be investigated must be defined by the experimenter.
